books.section: American Revolution and the New Nation (1775–1787)

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.
stimulus.text:
| Revolution | When | Political change | Social change |
| American Revolution | 1775–1783 | Independence from Britain; a republic replaces monarchy | Slavery continues; property-based political power largely intact |
| French Revolution | 1789–1799 | Monarchy overthrown; a republic proclaimed | Feudal privileges abolished; the Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaims equality |
| Haitian Revolution | 1791–1804 | Independence from France; a republic founded by formerly enslaved people | Slavery itself destroyed; the plantation system overthrown |

source: original; stimulus is an original data table compiled from the grounding books
stem: Using the table, which of the following best explains why historians treat the Haitian Revolution as the most socially radical of the three revolutions?

options.text: Haiti was the only one of the three revolutions to win independence from a European power.
options.misconception: All three broke with a European monarchy; America did so first.

options.text: Haiti was the only revolution fought with the help of a foreign army.
options.misconception: The American victory depended on French aid, and the French Revolution faced foreign invasion, not foreign help.

options.text: Haiti was the only revolution in which enslaved people fought on the side of their enslavers.
options.misconception: In Haiti the enslaved rose against their enslavers; that is the point of the revolution.

options.text: Haiti was the only revolution in which enslaved people themselves destroyed slavery and founded a republic.

rationales.A: All three broke with a European monarchy; America did so first.
rationales.B: The American victory depended on French aid, and the French Revolution faced foreign invasion, not foreign help.
rationales.C: In Haiti the enslaved rose against their enslavers; that is the point of the revolution.
rationales.D: The table's social row for Haiti is the only one that names the destruction of slavery itself: enslaved people rose in 1791, defeated the French planters and then Napoleon's army, and founded an independent republic in 1804. Background: in America the political break left slavery intact, and in France the revolution abolished feudal privilege but slavery in the colonies was restored under Napoleon. Only in Haiti did the people at the bottom of the social order remake the order itself.
rationales.general:
1. Find the social row for each revolution. America: slavery continues. France: feudal privilege falls. Haiti: slavery destroyed.
2. Ask who did the destroying in Haiti. Not reformers from above, but enslaved people themselves, rising in 1791.
3. Ask what they built. Not a new king or a new master, but a republic founded by the formerly enslaved.
4. Put it together. A revolution is socially radical when it changes who stands at the bottom — and only Haiti did that.
Remember: “radical” is not about how loud the fighting was — it is about how deep the change went.
